analogy.p: Think of xylem as a drinking straw: when you suck at the top (evaporation from the leaves), the whole column of liquid is pulled up in one continuous stream, and nothing flows down the straw. Phloem is more like a two-way delivery motorway with toll-booths: lorries (sucrose) are loaded at a depot (the leaf, the source) and delivered wherever they are needed (sinks), and the loading uses energy. The analogy breaks down because a straw is pulled by your mouth, but in a plant the pull comes from the Sun's energy evaporating water, and real phloem moves sap as a solution rather than separate vehicles.
analogy.t: A drinking straw and a motorway

bullets: **Root hair cells:** take up water by **osmosis** and mineral ions by **active transport**.
**Xylem:** transports **water and mineral ions** from the roots to the stem and leaves; made of dead cells strengthened with **lignin**; one-way (upwards).
**Phloem:** transports **dissolved sugars (sucrose)** from the leaves to the rest of the plant; made of living cells; **translocation** can go up and down.
**Transpiration:** the loss of water vapour from the leaves, which pulls a continuous **transpiration stream** up the xylem.
Typical marks: 1 mark to name the tissue; 2 to 3 marks to explain how a structure suits its function; 4 to 6 marks to describe the whole route water takes.
Link to other topics: osmosis and active transport (Topic 4.1), plant tissues and organs (4.2), photosynthesis (4.4), and the factors that change transpiration rate (next note).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA wants you to **describe how water and mineral ions get from the soil to the leaves** and **how sugars made in the leaves reach the rest of the plant**. That means knowing the structure and function of **root hair cells, xylem and phloem**, the processes of **transpiration** and **translocation**, and being able to link each structure to its job. Questions often give you an unfamiliar plant or a diagram and ask you to apply these ideas, so you need the ideas, not a memorised paragraph.

bullets: Diffusion is only fast enough over very short distances (a few cells), so a **mass flow system** is needed in large organisms.
Roots need **sugars** (made in leaves) for respiration, which provides energy for **active transport** of ions.
Leaves need **water** for photosynthesis and **mineral ions** (for example nitrate for amino acids and magnesium for chlorophyll).
Stems, roots and leaves are the **organs** that make up the **organ system for transport of substances** around the plant.
The transport tissues are arranged in **vascular bundles** (xylem and phloem together), which run through the roots, stem and leaf veins.
Plants have no heart or pump: movement is driven by **evaporation** (xylem) and by **active loading of sugars** (phloem).
core.p: A plant is multicellular and large, so most of its cells are **too far from the soil or the air** for substances to reach them by diffusion alone. Roots are underground and take in water and mineral ions, while the leaves are above ground where light is available to make sugars. Plants therefore need transport tissues to move water, minerals and sugars between these distant organs. Without them, leaves would run out of water and roots would run out of sugar for respiration.

bullets: **Large surface area** from the root hair: more space for water to enter by osmosis and ions by active transport.
**Thin cell wall** at the hair: a short distance for water to move through.
**Large permanent vacuole** containing cell sap with dissolved sugars and salts, keeping the **water potential inside lower than in the soil** so water moves in by osmosis.
**Many mitochondria** in the cytoplasm: release energy by respiration for **active transport** of mineral ions.
**No chloroplasts**: the cell is underground, so there is no light for photosynthesis.
Root hair cells are **short-lived** and are constantly replaced as the root grows.
Root hairs are found a little behind the root tip, where the root is still growing into new soil.
core.h: Root hair cells: structure and adaptations
core.p: Root hair cells are specialised cells on the surface of roots. Each has a long, thin projection (the root hair) that sticks out into the soil. This gives the cell a **very large surface area** for absorbing water and mineral ions, and the hair is so thin that the **diffusion/osmosis distance is short**. Their job is to take in water and dissolved mineral ions from the soil as efficiently as possible.

bullets: **Osmosis:** diffusion of water through a partially permeable membrane from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution.
**Active transport:** movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient) using **energy released by respiration**.
Active transport allows the plant to **absorb ions even when soil concentration is very low**, for example nitrate and magnesium.
If the soil is waterlogged there is little oxygen, so aerobic respiration slows and **less energy is available for active transport**; ion uptake falls.
If the soil is very salty (or the plant is given too much fertiliser) the soil water can have a lower water potential than the cell, so water leaves the root by osmosis and the plant wilts.
Once inside, water and ions move across the root cortex into the **xylem** in the centre of the root.
core.h: How water and mineral ions enter the root
core.p: Water moves from the soil into the root hair cell by **osmosis**: it travels from a region of **higher water potential** (dilute soil water) to a region of **lower water potential** (the more concentrated cell sap), across a **partially permeable membrane**. Osmosis is a passive process, so it needs no energy. Mineral ions are usually at a **lower concentration in the soil than in the root hair cell**, so they cannot enter by diffusion. They are taken up by **active transport**, which moves them **against the concentration gradient** using energy from respiration and carrier proteins in the cell membrane.

bullets: **Dead, hollow cells with no end walls** form a continuous tube, so water flows through with little resistance.
**Lignin** is laid down in spirals or rings: it makes the tubes strong, so they do not collapse under the low pressure (tension) inside them, and it also **supports the plant**.
Lignin is waterproof, so water cannot leak out through the walls of the tubes.
Water and ions move **one way only: upwards** from the roots to the leaves.
Xylem is made of **dead** cells, so it has **no active transport and needs no energy** itself.
Pits (small gaps) in the walls let water move sideways between xylem vessels and to surrounding cells.
In a stem the xylem and phloem lie together in **vascular bundles**; xylem is on the inner side of each bundle.
core.p: Xylem tissue is a system of long, hollow tubes that carries **water and mineral ions from the roots up to the stem and leaves**. Xylem cells are **dead** when they are mature. Their end walls break down, leaving a continuous empty tube with **no cytoplasm or organelles** to block the flow. The walls are thickened and strengthened with a waterproof, tough substance called **lignin**.

bullets: **Step 1:** water enters the root hair cells by **osmosis** and crosses the root to the xylem.
**Step 2:** water evaporates from the surface of the **mesophyll cells** into the **air spaces** inside the leaf.
**Step 3:** water vapour **diffuses out through the stomata** down a concentration gradient (the air spaces are more humid than the outside air).
**Step 4:** loss of water from the leaf means less water in the leaf cells, so water is **drawn up the xylem** to replace it.
**Step 5:** because water molecules are attracted to each other (**cohesion**) they are pulled up as a continuous column, like a chain.
The stream is **continuous**: it only stops if the xylem is broken or air bubbles interrupt the column.
About 99% of water taken in by a plant is lost by transpiration; only a small amount is used in photosynthesis and to keep cells turgid.
core.h: Transpiration and the transpiration stream (step by step)
core.p: **Transpiration** is the loss of water vapour from the leaves (mainly through the stomata). It is essentially evaporation of water from the surface of the spongy mesophyll cells inside the leaf followed by diffusion of water vapour out through open stomata. This removal of water creates a pull that draws more water up the xylem, giving a continuous **transpiration stream** from roots to leaves. The movement is driven by the Sun's energy, which evaporates the water, not by the plant using up its own energy.

bullets: Supplies **water for photosynthesis** in the leaf.
Carries **mineral ions** (nitrate, magnesium and others) up from the roots to where they are needed.
Provides water to keep cells **turgid**, which supports the plant and keeps leaves held out to the light.
The evaporation of water has a **cooling effect** on the leaves in hot weather.
Cost: if water is lost faster than it can be absorbed, cells lose turgor and the plant **wilts**; severe water shortage can kill it.
Trade-off: stomata must open for **CO2 intake**, but open stomata let **water vapour escape**.
core.h: Why transpiration is useful (and the cost)
core.p: Transpiration is not just a leak. It brings real benefits to the plant, but it also costs water, so plants have to balance the two. If water loss is faster than uptake, the plant wilts. Plants reduce the problem by closing stomata when water is short, which unfortunately also stops carbon dioxide entering for photosynthesis.

bullets: **Sieve tube elements** are living but have lost most organelles, leaving more room for the sap to flow.
**Sieve plates** are perforated end walls with pores that let the sugary solution (sap) pass from cell to cell.
**Companion cells** have a nucleus and many **mitochondria**; they provide the energy (ATP) needed to **load sugars into the phloem** by active transport.
Phloem carries dissolved **sucrose** (not glucose) because sucrose is soluble, transportable and less chemically reactive than glucose.
Phloem tubes are thin-walled compared with xylem and have **no lignin**.
Phloem is on the **outer side** of the vascular bundle in a stem.
core.p: Phloem tissue transports **dissolved sugars (mainly sucrose) and other organic substances** such as amino acids around the plant. Unlike xylem, phloem is made of **living cells**. The tubes are formed from **sieve tube elements** joined end to end, with the end walls containing pores to make **sieve plates**. Each sieve tube element has very little cytoplasm and no nucleus, and is supported by a **companion cell**.

bullets: **Sources:** photosynthesising leaves (and storage organs releasing stored sugar in spring).
**Sinks:** growing root and shoot tips, flowers, developing fruit and seeds, and storage organs such as roots, tubers and bulbs.
Sugar is moved as **sucrose** and may be converted to **starch** for storage or to cellulose for cell walls at the sink.
Translocation is an **active process**: it needs energy from respiration (in companion cells) to load sugars.
In spring, sugar stored in roots can be moved **upwards** to help new buds grow; in summer, sugars from leaves go **down** to roots.
The movement is of a **solution (sap)** along the phloem tubes; the direction depends on where the source and sink are.
core.h: Translocation: moving sugars from source to sink
core.p: **Translocation** is the movement of dissolved sugars from the leaves, where they are made by photosynthesis, to the parts of the plant that need them for **respiration, growth or storage**. The leaves are the **source** (sugar is made or released) and the places that use or store sugar are the **sinks**. Translocation requires **energy** because sugar is actively loaded into the phloem, and it can move **in both directions** (up and down the plant), unlike xylem transport.

bullets: **Substance carried:** xylem = water and mineral ions; phloem = dissolved sugars (sucrose) and amino acids.
**Direction:** xylem = one way (up); phloem = both ways (up and down).
**Cells:** xylem = dead, hollow, no end walls; phloem = living sieve tube elements with sieve plates and companion cells.
**Strengthening:** xylem has lignin; phloem does not.
**Energy:** xylem uses no energy of its own (driven by evaporation); phloem translocation needs energy.
**Process names:** xylem = transpiration stream; phloem = translocation.
**Position in a stem bundle:** xylem inside, phloem outside.
core.p: Examiners love comparison questions because they test whether you really know the difference between the two tissues. Always compare the same feature in both (for example both cell types, both directions) rather than describing each separately. The key contrasts are what is carried, the direction, the cell type (dead or living) and what drives the movement.

bullets: Coloured dye (for example food colouring) moves up the **xylem** and stains the vascular bundles, so cross-sections show dots/rings of colour.
Cutting a thin transverse section and viewing under a microscope shows the **xylem and phloem arrangement**.
To measure transpiration by mass: cover the soil and pot with a plastic bag so only the plant loses water, then record mass at regular intervals.
Rate of water loss = **change in mass ÷ time** (for example g per hour).
Control variables: same plant, same light, temperature, humidity and air movement.
Make a repeat and calculate a **mean** to improve reliability.
If a plant is ringed (a ring of bark with phloem is removed) sugars build up above the ring, which suggests phloem carries sugar. (Know the idea, not the full method.)
core.p: You may be asked how to show where water or sugar travels in a plant. A classic investigation is to stand a stem (for example celery or a white carnation) in water containing a coloured dye, then cut sections. The dye shows up in the xylem, which is where water travels. Another standard idea is to measure mass loss of a potted plant (with the soil surface covered) to estimate how much water has been lost by transpiration.

bullets: **Osmosis (4.1.3):** water moves into root hair cells because the cell sap has a lower water potential than the soil water.
**Active transport (4.1.3):** needs respiration, so oxygen and glucose supply affect ion uptake.
**Photosynthesis (4.4):** water from the xylem and sugars carried away by the phloem; sugar build-up could slow photosynthesis.
**Respiration:** roots respire the sugar delivered by phloem to release energy.
**Cell differentiation:** xylem and phloem cells are specialised cells that develop from meristems.
**Environmental factors:** temperature, light, humidity and air movement affect transpiration (see stomata note).
**Data skills:** be ready to calculate rates (mass or volume per unit time), percentage change and means from tables.
core.h: Common links to other topics and Higher-tier thinking
core.p: Questions on this topic rarely stand alone. They often mix transport with osmosis, active transport, photosynthesis, respiration or the effect of environmental conditions. A grade 9 answer picks the right idea from each topic and explains the chain of cause and effect. For instance, a waterlogged plant takes up fewer ions because there is less oxygen for respiration, so less energy for active transport.

exam: Command words: **State/Name** (1 mark, just the term), **Describe** (say what happens, in order), **Explain** (give a reason using 'because', 'so', 'which means'), **Compare** (similarity and difference for both items).
1 mark: correct tissue or process name. 2 marks: structure plus link to function, for example 'long root hair, so large surface area for absorption'.
3 to 4 marks, route of water: root hair cell by osmosis, through the root to xylem, up the xylem, to the leaf, evaporates from mesophyll, diffuses out of the stomata.
For ion uptake always write: **active transport, against the concentration gradient, needs energy from respiration**, via mitochondria.
Always state **direction** in xylem vs phloem comparisons: xylem one way (up), phloem both ways.
Use 'dead' and 'living' correctly, and mention **lignin** for xylem and **sieve plates/companion cells** for phloem.
Calculation tip: rate = change ÷ time. Show the working and give units such as g per hour or mm³ per minute.
If a question gives data after an experiment, compare actual numbers (with units) from the table or graph and say what the trend shows.
6 mark extended answers: organise as root, stem, leaf. Include osmosis, active transport, xylem, evaporation, stomata, and say what happens to sugars (phloem).
Do not say 'water goes up because it is hot'. Say: evaporation from the leaves creates a pull (transpiration stream) which draws water up the xylem.
Link structure to function every time: do not just list features.

mistakes.r: Xylem carries water and mineral ions; phloem carries dissolved sugars (sucrose).
mistakes.w: Xylem carries sugar (or food) around the plant.

mistakes.r: Transpiration is the loss of water vapour from the leaves (evaporation then diffusion out of the stomata).
mistakes.w: Transpiration is water going into the roots.

mistakes.r: Translocation moves sugars in both directions, from sources to sinks.
mistakes.w: Translocation only moves sugar up the plant.

mistakes.r: Water enters by osmosis; mineral ions enter by active transport (against the concentration gradient, using energy from respiration).
mistakes.w: Root hair cells take in minerals by osmosis.

mistakes.r: Mature xylem cells are dead and hollow with no end walls; they are strengthened with lignin.
mistakes.w: Xylem is made of living cells with a nucleus.

mistakes.r: Active transport uses energy released by respiration, so it needs mitochondria and (usually) oxygen.
mistakes.w: Active transport does not need oxygen or energy.

mistakes.r: Evaporation from the leaves pulls water up the xylem; there is no pump.
mistakes.w: Plants 'suck up' water using a pump.

mistakes.r: Phloem sieve tubes are living; companion cells provide energy for translocation.
mistakes.w: Phloem cells are dead like xylem.

mistakes.r: They have no chloroplasts because they are underground with no light.

summary: AQA 4.2.3: you must describe the structure and function of root hair cells, xylem and phloem, and explain transpiration (the transpiration stream) and translocation, including how water and mineral ions enter roots by osmosis and active transport. It matters because it explains how a large plant with no pump keeps its leaves supplied with water and its roots supplied with sugar.

terms.d: A specialised plant cell with a long thin projection that gives a large surface area for absorbing water and mineral ions from the soil.
The diffusion of water from a dilute solution to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
The movement of substances from a more dilute solution to a more concentrated solution (against a concentration gradient), which needs energy from respiration.
Plant tissue made of dead, hollow cells strengthened with lignin that transports water and mineral ions from the roots to the stem and leaves.
Plant tissue made of living cells that transports dissolved sugars in both directions around the plant.
A strong, waterproof substance that strengthens the walls of xylem cells and supports the plant.
The loss of water vapour from the leaves of a plant, mainly through the stomata.
The continuous movement of water from the roots, up the xylem and out of the leaves.
The movement of dissolved sugars (sucrose) from the leaves to other parts of the plant in the phloem, using energy.
A perforated end wall between phloem sieve tube elements that allows sap to flow from cell to cell.
A cell next to a phloem sieve tube element that has a nucleus and many mitochondria and supplies energy for loading sugars.
A part of the plant (such as a photosynthesising leaf) where sugars are made or released into the phloem.
A part of the plant (such as roots, fruits or growing tips) that uses or stores sugars delivered by the phloem.
Small pores, mainly in the lower epidermis of the leaf, through which gases and water vapour move.
A group of xylem and phloem tissue running together through the roots, stems and leaves.
Describes a plant cell that is full of water and pressing against the cell wall, which gives support.
The attraction between water molecules that helps pull them up the xylem as a continuous column.

worked.ans: Water enters the root hair cells by osmosis and passes across the root into the xylem. It is carried up the xylem to the leaves, where it evaporates from the mesophyll cells and the water vapour diffuses out of the stomata. This is transpiration, and it pulls a continuous stream of water up the plant.
worked.q: Describe how water moves from the soil to the air through a plant. (4 marks)
steps: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis (1).
It moves across the root into the xylem, which carries it up the stem to the leaves (1).
Water evaporates from the surface of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces (1).
Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata; this loss pulls more water up the xylem (1).

worked.ans: The concentration of mineral ions in the soil is lower than in the root hair cell, so diffusion would move them out, not in. Active transport moves ions against the concentration gradient and uses energy from respiration, so the plant can take in the ions it needs.
worked.q: Explain why mineral ions are taken into root hair cells by active transport and not diffusion. (3 marks)
steps: Concentration of ions in soil is lower than in the cell (1).
Diffusion only moves substances down a concentration gradient, so it cannot move ions in (1).
Active transport moves them against the gradient using energy from respiration (1).
